claims.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys have strong high-temperature mechanical properties and thermal stability.
Conventional refractory HEAs possess irradiation resistance suitable for nuclear applications.
Tungsten and tantalum are high-neutron-activation elements.
Tungsten or tantalum in refractory HEAs produces long-lived radioactive isotopes under neutron irradiation.
Vanadium and titanium are low-activation substitutes for tungsten or tantalum.
Reducing or partially replacing tungsten or tantalum with vanadium or titanium can preserve a BCC solid-solution structure.
Fusion plasma-facing components must operate at temperatures of at least 1000 K.
Fusion plasma-facing components are exposed to energetic plasma species and neutrons.
Fusion plasma-facing materials require low activation and good thermomechanical performance.
A single-phase BCC-dominated microstructure supports high-temperature mechanical strength.
A single-phase BCC-dominated microstructure supports irradiation tolerance.
Reducing the concentration of high-activation elements will reduce the production of long-lived radioactive isotopes during neutron irradiation.
Configurational entropy promotes solid-solution formation in HEAs.
High configurational entropy slows atomic diffusion.
Slowed atomic diffusion stabilizes the altered HEA microstructure under fusion-reactor conditions.
Maintaining high configurational entropy after substitution preserves high-temperature mechanical and irradiation-resistant properties.
The tailored alloy will form fewer long-lived activation products than the original refractory HEA under neutron exposure.
The tailored alloy will have high-temperature mechanical performance comparable to the original refractory HEA.
Conventional tungsten- or tantalum-containing refractory HEAs are used as plasma-facing components and suffer from long-term radioactivation.
